lead: A centrifugal pump is a rotodynamic pump: a spinning impeller throws water outward, and a widening casing slows that water so its speed becomes pressure. One shaft and one impeller move large flows smoothly, so you meet the pump in apartment overhead tanks, irrigation pumpsets, borewell submersibles, power-plant cooling lines and coffee machines. This chapter names the parts, follows the water from sump to tank, and shows why the casing must be full of water before the motor starts.
prereq: You need pressure and its variation with depth (Unit 1), Bernoulli's equation (Unit 3), and the pump grouping in 7.1.

sections.h3: The parts, and the job each one does

blocks.text: A centrifugal pump has two moving parts: the impeller and its shaft. Everything else guides water or holds pressure.

items: Suction pipe: carries water from sump to impeller under partial vacuum, so joints must be airtight.

Foot valve and strainer: the foot valve is a one-way valve at the bottom of the suction pipe; water enters upward and cannot run back, so the casing stays full between starts. The strainer keeps out sand and leaves.
Impeller and eye: a disc with curved vanes. The eye is the hole at its centre; water enters along the axis and leaves at the outer edge, radially.
Casing: an airtight shell that collects water and guides it to the delivery pipe.
Shaft, gland and stuffing box: the shaft brings power from the motor; the gland seals the gap where it passes through the casing while letting it turn.

blocks.text: An open impeller has vanes on one plate with no cover discs: it passes muddy water without choking, at lower efficiency. A semi-open impeller has one cover disc. A closed impeller traps water between two cover discs, gives the best efficiency, and suits clean water.

A volute casing is a spiral whose flow area grows towards the delivery branch. A vortex chamber is a circular casing of constant area with a separate diffuser pipe. A diffuser ring is fixed guide vanes around the impeller that slow the water; diffuser and multistage pumps use it.

items: Prime: fill the casing and suction pipe with water; the foot valve holds it in.
Start with the delivery valve closed. The impeller spins in the water-filled casing.
The vanes push water outward; a low-pressure region forms at the eye.
Atmospheric pressure on the sump pushes water up the suction pipe. The pump does not suck; the atmosphere pushes.
The casing slows the water: velocity head falls, pressure head rises. Open the delivery valve slowly.

blocks.where: p_eye is absolute pressure at the eye (Pa); p_atm is atmospheric pressure (about 101 325 Pa at sea level); ρ is density (1000 kg/m³ for water); g = 9.81 m/s²; H_s is suction lift from sump surface to pump centreline (m); h_fs is head lost in strainer, foot valve and suction pipe (m).

blocks.text: Priming is not optional. A dry casing holds air, and the same head in metres of air gives a pressure smaller than in metres of water by the density ratio, about 1.2/1000 — far too small to lift water. A dry pump runs hot and delivers nothing.

Water leaves the vane tips at V₁, often 10 to 25 m/s. That speed is useless in a pipe, where friction loss grows with V². The casing diffuses it: area increases, V falls to V₂, and Bernoulli gives the pressure rise.
p₂ = p₁ + ½ρ(V₁² − V₂²) − ρ g h_L
blocks.where: p₁, V₁ are at the impeller outlet; p₂, V₂ at the delivery branch; ρ is density; h_L is head lost inside the casing. The casing adds no energy; it only converts velocity head into pressure head.

sections.h3: Why the suction side decides the layout

blocks.text: Atmospheric pressure at sea level balances 10.33 m of water — the absolute ceiling on suction lift. The strainer, foot valve and pipe friction take 1 to 3 m, so a real pump sits within about 6 to 7 m above the sump level.

So the pump sits near the sump, not near the tank. Pushing water on the delivery side is easy; pulling it on the suction side is limited by the atmosphere. A Chennai apartment pump sits at ground level beside the sump and pushes to the roof tank.

A deep borewell breaks the limit by going down instead of pulling up. A multistage pump keys many impellers on one shaft in one casing; each stage passes water to the next, so each adds head. At ground level it is a deep-well pump; lowered under water it is a submersible. Use a closed impeller for clear water, an open one for sandy water, a single volute for large flow at low head, and several stages for small flow at high head.

figure.caption: The water path from sump to tank: atmospheric pressure pushes water up the suction pipe into the low-pressure eye, the spinning vanes add energy, and the widening volute slows the water and turns speed into pressure.

spec.aria: Water moves from the suction pipe to the impeller eye, gains energy in the vanes, and leaves through the volute casing to the delivery pipe.

examples.question: A pump lifts water from a sump 3 m below its centreline and delivers to a tank whose surface is 12 m above it. The foot valve and strainer lose 0.5 m of head at design flow. Take p_atm = 101 325 Pa, ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². (a) Find the absolute eye pressure. (b) Find the static head. (c) A dry casing develops the same 3 m of head in air of density 1.2 kg/m³ — what water column could that support, and why prime?
steps: Flow path: sump → strainer and foot valve → suction pipe → eye → vanes → volute → delivery pipe → tank, as in the figure.
That is below atmospheric, which is what keeps water coming in.
(b) Static head = 12 + 3 = 15 m of water; pipe friction is extra.
(c) 3 m of air gives 1.2 × 9.81 × 3 = 35.3 Pa, a water column of 35.3/(1000 × 9.81) = 3.6 mm.
3.6 mm cannot lift water 3 m. Priming fills the casing with water, about 830 times denser than air, so the same head gives a pressure large enough to lift water.
examples.answer: Eye pressure 66 990 Pa absolute (about 67 kPa), static head 15 m, and a dry casing lifts water only 3.6 mm — so prime before starting.
examples.check:
patm = 101325.0
rho = 1000.0
g = 9.81
hs = 3.0
hf = 0.5
p_eye = patm - rho * g * (hs + hf)
print(round(p_eye, 2))
H_static = 12.0 + 3.0
print(round(H_static, 2))
rho_air = 1.2
p_air = rho_air * g * 3.0
h_water_mm = p_air / (rho * g) * 1000.0
print(round(h_water_mm, 2))

traps: Priming is not optional; a dry casing spins air, too light to lift water more than a few millimetres.
The foot valve is not the delivery valve. It is a non-return valve at the bottom of the suction pipe that keeps the casing full, so priming survives a stop.
The volute adds no energy; it converts velocity head into pressure head. The energy came from the shaft through the impeller.
Water enters the eye axially and leaves radially; saying it enters radially loses marks.
Atmospheric head is 10.33 m, not the permitted suction lift; losses cut the usable lift to about 6 to 7 m.

quiz.q: Name the part at the bottom of the suction pipe that keeps the casing full when the pump stops.
quiz.a: The foot valve — a one-way valve that lets water flow up and prevents it running back.

quiz.q: What is the eye of the impeller?
quiz.a: The central opening of the impeller through which water enters along the shaft axis.

quiz.q: Why is pressure low at the eye while the pump runs?
quiz.a: The vanes throw water outward, so water leaves the centre faster than it arrives and a low-pressure region forms. Atmospheric pressure on the sump then pushes fresh water up the suction pipe into it.

quiz.q: The volute's flow area grows towards the delivery branch. What happens to velocity and pressure, and why?
quiz.a: Area increases, so velocity falls and pressure rises, as Bernoulli requires for a diffuser. The casing adds no energy; it converts the impeller's kinetic energy into pressure.

quiz.q: A pump centreline is 2.5 m above the sump surface and suction losses are 0.4 m. Take p_atm = 101 325 Pa, ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². Find the eye pressure in kPa.
A pump is to be fixed with 8 m suction lift where p_atm = 90 kPa. Comment.
quiz.a: Atmospheric head = 90 000/(1000 × 9.81) = 9.17 m. An 8 m lift leaves 1.17 m for losses and eye velocity head; any real loss drives the eye towards vapour pressure, so the pump cavitates. Reduce the lift or lower the pump.

quiz.q: Why is a borewell pump lowered under water instead of kept at ground level, and what does a multistage unit do?
quiz.a: Atmospheric head caps suction lift at 10.33 m, and losses cut it to about 6 to 7 m; borewell water may be deeper, so ground-level suction cannot reach it. Lowering the pump puts the eye under water. Several impellers on one shaft pass water stage to stage, each adding head.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real volute design uses computational fluid dynamics, because a badly matched volute recirculates water at part load and wastes power. Variable-frequency drives make motor speed follow demand, and the affinity laws predict the new duty point without a fresh test. In micro-hydro, the same machine run backwards is a pump-as-turbine.
